chief_complaint: periumbilical pain migrating to right lower abdominal quadrant with fever and vomiting
hpi_details: 26M presents with 18-hour history of abdominal pain that began as a dull, vague ache around his belly button (periumbilical) 12 hours ago, but over the past 6 hours has shifted and intensified into a sharp, constant, excruciating pain localized to his right lower quadrant (RLQ). Associated with anorexia, nausea, one episode of vomiting after the pain started, and low-grade fever.
ideas: thinks his appendix is infected and about to burst
concerns: worried about needing emergency surgery right away
expectations: wants IV pain killers, antibiotics, and an operation to remove his appendix safely
pmh: No prior surgery or health conditions

investigation_events.availability_message: The urgent appendicitis results are now available; analgesia, IV fluids, antibiotics, and surgical consultation should not be delayed.

results.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
results.value: Dilated appendix measuring 11 mm with an appendicolith and periappendiceal fat stranding; no abscess or free air

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Appendicitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes keeping the patient NPO, IV fluid resuscitation, IV analgesia, pre-operative antibiotics, and urgent surgical consultation for appendectomy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: periumbilical pain migrating to right lower abdominal quadrant with fever and vomiting

Key HPI features: 26M presents with 18-hour history of abdominal pain that began as a dull, vague ache around his belly button (periumbilical) 12 hours ago, but over the past 6 hours has shifted and intensified into a sharp, constant, excruciating pain localized to his right lower quadrant (RLQ). Associated with anorexia, nausea, one episode of vomiting after the pain started, and low-grade fever.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 38.2C, HR 98, BP 124/78. Abdominal exam reveals localized involuntary guarding, rebound tenderness, and maximal point tenderness at McBurney's point (1/3 distance from right anterior superior iliac spine to umbilicus). Positive Rovsing's sign (LLQ palpation causes RLQ pain), positive Psoas sign (pain on right hip extension), and positive Obturator sign (pain on internal rotation of flexed right hip). Bloods: WBC 15,800 /uL with 86% neutrophils (left shift), CRP 42 mg/L. Abdominal CT with IV contrast demonstrates an enlarged, non-compressible appendix measuring 11 mm with periappendiceal fat stranding and an appendicolith at the base.
Relevant background/PMH: No prior surgery or health conditions
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Appendicitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Mesenteric adenitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Diffuse rigid abdomen (suggests perforation).
management_principles: Keep patient NPO, initiate IV normal saline maintenance hydration, and administer IV opioid analgesia
Start pre-operative broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering enteric Gram-negatives and anaerobes (Cefoxitin 2g IV or Cefazolin + Metronidazole)
Obtain urgent General Surgery consultation for laparoscopic appendectomy within 12-24 hours
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

learning_objectives: Recognize classical visceral-to-somatic pain migration from periumbilical region to McBurney's point
Elicit and interpret peritoneal irritation signs (Rovsing's, Psoas, Obturator, rebound tenderness)
Execute pre-operative preparation protocol including NPO status, IV antibiotics, and fluid resuscitation
Outline surgical anatomy and laparoscopic approach for acute appendicitis

teaching.one_liner: Obstruction of the appendiceal lumen causing pain that classically starts vaguely around the navel and migrates to the right lower quadrant as inflammation reaches the peritoneum.

must_ask.say: Did the pain start around your belly button and then move to your lower right side?
When exactly did the pain start?
Have you lost your appetite, felt nauseated, or vomited?
Does moving, coughing, or pressing on your belly make the pain worse?
Have you ever had abdominal surgery, or felt pain like this before?

history.answer: My stomach has been hurting really badly on the lower right side, and I threw up earlier today.
It started about 18 hours ago as a dull ache around my belly button, but over the last 6 hours it moved down to my lower right side and became much sharper and agonizing.
At first it was vague and centered around my belly button, but then it shifted over to my lower right belly.
No, it doesn't travel to my back, shoulder, or down to my groin; it stays focused right here in my lower right belly.
It began as a dull, vague ache, but now it feels like a sharp, constant, unbearable pain.
It started at about a 3 out of 10, but right now it is easily an 8 or 9 out of 10.
Walking, coughing, or any bumps on the drive here made it intensely worse; lying down completely still with my knees curled up helps slightly.
No, I have never felt pain like this before.
I lost my appetite completely, felt very sick to my stomach, and threw up once after the pain got worse; there was no blood in the vomit.
I haven't had diarrhea or any blood in my stool, but I haven't been able to pass gas or have a bowel movement today.
Yes, I have been feeling hot and feverish with mild chills since this morning.
No, my eyes and skin haven't turned yellow, and my urine and stool look normal in color.
No, I have no pain or burning when I urinate, no blood in my urine, and I'm not going more frequently than usual.
No, I haven't felt faint, dizzy, or lightheaded at all.
No chest pain, no tightness, and no shortness of breath whatsoever.
I had regular home-cooked food last night, nothing particularly greasy or spicy, and I haven't had any alcohol.
No, I haven't taken any pain medicine, anti-inflammatory pills, or aspirin.
No, my heart is completely normal and I've never had palpitations, irregular beats, or blood vessel issues.
I think my appendix might be infected and on the verge of bursting.
I'm really worried that I might need emergency surgery right away.
I'm hoping to get IV pain medicine, antibiotics, and an operation to remove my appendix safely.
I don't have any chronic medical conditions or health problems.
I have never had any surgeries and I've never been admitted to a hospital before.
I don't take any regular prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or latex.
No, I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink socially once in a while, but I haven't had any alcohol recently.
I work as a software engineer and live alone in an apartment.
No one in my family has serious digestive problems, bowel diseases, or chronic illnesses.
I am in a monogamous relationship, and I have never had any sexually transmitted infections.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg, pulse 98 beats per minute, temperature 38.2°C (100.8°F), respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Patient appears acutely uncomfortable and lies still on the examination table with his right hip slightly flexed to reduce abdominal tension.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor, and sclerae are completely anicteric.
Abdomen is flat and symmetric without visible distension, rashes, or surgical scars.
Hypoactive bowel sounds are heard across all four quadrants.
Localized involuntary guarding and severe focal tenderness are present in the right lower quadrant, while upper quadrants are soft and non-tender.
Pronounced rebound tenderness is elicited specifically in the right lower quadrant.
Maximal tenderness is located at McBurney's point, with positive Rovsing's sign, positive psoas sign, and positive obturator sign on the right.
No costovertebral angle tenderness is elicited on either side.
Normal sphincter tone with tenderness palpated along the right pelvic peritoneal reflection, and no blood or melena on the glove.
